courseLedger.name: Personal & Professional Development

contentRead.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
contentRead.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
contentRead.discipline: Academic writing
contentRead.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
contentRead.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

courseLedger.contribution: Required first-year academic research literacy, writing, personal development and civic project.

courseLedger.name: Sustainability Essentials I

contentRead.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
contentRead.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
contentRead.discipline: Sustainability science; Applied mathematics; Chemistry; Physics
contentRead.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
contentRead.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

courseLedger.contribution: Actual mechanics, stress/strain, materials, thermodynamics, chemical systems, modelling and biopolymer strength experiments support environmental/material reasoning; not complete structural mechanics.

courseLedger.name: Sustainability Essentials II

contentRead.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
contentRead.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
contentRead.discipline: Physics; Chemistry; Materials science; Sustainability studies
contentRead.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
contentRead.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

courseLedger.contribution: Actual waves, spectroscopy, chemistry, materials structure, stress-strain/Mohr circle and practical evidence support technical sustainability; not a whole building-physics sequence.

courseLedger.name: Building with Nature

contentRead.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
contentRead.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
contentRead.discipline: Ecological engineering; Environmental planning; Ecology
contentRead.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
contentRead.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

courseLedger.contribution: Direct nature-based infrastructure/intervention design, urban nature and practical model walls; not a building-design studio.

courseLedger.name: Living with Water

contentRead.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
contentRead.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
contentRead.discipline: Water management; Environmental governance; Delta sustainability
contentRead.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience
contentRead.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development

courseLedger.contribution: Direct delta/urban-water adaptation, resilient infrastructure and site-based evaluation with governance; context-sensitive adaptation project.

courseLedger.name: Climate Change

contentRead.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
contentRead.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
contentRead.discipline: Climate science; Environmental studies; Climate governance
contentRead.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
contentRead.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

courseLedger.contribution: Climate science, building/transport impacts and climate-adaptive planning; stakeholder interview and communication, not thermal simulation.

courseLedger.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy

contentRead.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
contentRead.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
contentRead.discipline: Sustainability science; Industrial ecology; Life-cycle engineering and management
contentRead.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
contentRead.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

courseLedger.contribution: Direct integrated life-cycle/circular assessment of products/processes, resources/costs and environmental impacts; no building-specific brief guaranteed.

courseLedger.name: Earth Observation

contentRead.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
contentRead.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
contentRead.discipline: Geographic information science; Remote sensing; Environmental science
contentRead.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
contentRead.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design

courseLedger.contribution: Direct GIS/geospatial databases/remote sensing/spatial visualization and collaborative environmental inquiry; not architectural BIM.

courseLedger.name: Spatial Planning

contentRead.description2: Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.

courseLedger.contribution: Description supports spatial engineering, GIS/remote sensing and hands-on disaster/agriculture/environmental projects. Full stated scope considered; do not infer architectural studio or land-use law.

courseLedger.name: Energy & Sustainability

contentRead.description2: Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.
contentRead.profile: Studies renewable-energy resources, conversion technologies and their integration into sustainable energy systems. Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass resources are evaluated through physical principles, resource availability and generation potential. Storage, electricity grids and demand management connect individual technologies to system reliability. Quantitative exercises, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work develop the ability to assess energy options in practical environmental and economic contexts.
contentRead.discipline: Energy engineering; Renewable-energy systems; Sustainability science; Applied physics
contentRead.topics: Energy demand and renewable resources; Solar radiation and energy yield; Solar thermal and photovoltaic generation; Wind energy; Hydropower; Geothermal energy; Biomass, biogas and biofuels; Electricity grids; Energy storage; Batteries and pumped storage; Smart grids and system integration; Demand management; Mini-grids; Energy-system environmental and economic constraints
contentRead.methods: Renewable-energy resource and yield calculations; Polysun energy-system modelling; Hydropower sizing; Laboratory experimentation on renewable-energy systems; Energy-storage comparison; Mini-grid analysis and design

courseLedger.contribution: Actual energy resource/yield calculations, Polysun modelling, renewable experiments, storage and mini-grid design; partially relevant energy methods, not full building-services engineering.

courseLedger.name: Renewable System Design

contentRead.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

courseLedger.contribution: Description supports energy-demand reduction/clean-energy design with technical/economic partner report. No building or HVAC project guaranteed.

courseLedger.name: Public Economics

contentRead.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
contentRead.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
contentRead.discipline: Public economics; Political economy
contentRead.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
contentRead.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

courseLedger.contribution: Actual publicgoods/externalities, collectivechoice/spending/taxation and data-informed policyresearch support urban infrastructure/sustainability decisions; no realestatevaluation or constructionfinance inferred.

courseLedger.name: Governance of Sustainability

contentRead.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
contentRead.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
contentRead.discipline: Environmental governance; Public policy; Political science
contentRead.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
contentRead.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

courseLedger.contribution: Direct stakeholder/governance/participation/justice and policy evaluation/advice on a Zeeland sustainability issue; supports urban systems, not urban design by itself.

courseLedger.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation

contentRead.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
contentRead.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
contentRead.discipline: Environmental chemistry; Materials recycling; Environmental biotechnology
contentRead.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
contentRead.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

courseLedger.contribution: Actual recycling/material recovery/remediation laboratories, microscopy/material characterization support circular material inquiry; not construction-material structural testing.

courseLedger.name: Earth's Resources

contentRead.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

courseLedger.contribution: Description supports resource/environment geoscience research, geothermal/nuclear storage/CO2capture literature and conference report; no property-development or architecture content inferred.

courseLedger.name: Consumer Product Design

contentRead.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
contentRead.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
contentRead.discipline: Product design; Product and process development; Sustainable design
contentRead.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
contentRead.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Actual user interviews, concepts/specifications, experimentation, quantitative models, prototyping, fabrication/scaling/circularity/cost analysis. Material design response but consumer products, not architectural design.

courseLedger.name: Mathematical Methods

contentRead.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
contentRead.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
contentRead.discipline: Mathematics; Calculus; Applied mathematics
contentRead.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
contentRead.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Single-variable calculus/differential equations and Mathematica dynamic-model project; strongest direct calculus counterpart, not spatial structural design.

courseLedger.name: Research Methods & Statistics

contentRead.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
contentRead.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
contentRead.discipline: Research methodology; Applied statistics
contentRead.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
contentRead.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

courseLedger.contribution: Actual statistical/empirical research design, sampling/survey/experiments, introductory regression and substantial R-based project; partial quantitative-method correspondence.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Data Science

contentRead.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
contentRead.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
contentRead.discipline: Data science
contentRead.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
contentRead.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

courseLedger.contribution: R cleaning/visualization of tabular/text/spatial data and actual research project; spatial-data tools complementary, not a building-specific database.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Sociology

contentRead.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
contentRead.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
contentRead.discipline: Sociology
contentRead.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
contentRead.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

courseLedger.contribution: Social structures, inequality and sociological theory contextualize user needs and urban society; no urban sociology specialization assumed.

courseLedger.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

contentRead.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
contentRead.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
contentRead.discipline: Qualitative research methodology; Social research
contentRead.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
contentRead.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

courseLedger.contribution: Actual qualitative research design, interviewing, observation, visual/participatory media and coding in team inquiry; partial research-method counterpart, not architectural design methodology.

courseLedger.name: Introduction to Economics

contentRead.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
contentRead.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
contentRead.discipline: Microeconomics; Macroeconomics
contentRead.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
contentRead.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

courseLedger.contribution: Actual microeconomic supply/demand,consumerchoice,production/costs/markets andmacroeconomic models precedePublicEconomics. Supports urban-development policycontext; no realestatevaluation.

courseLedger.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy

contentRead.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
contentRead.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
contentRead.discipline: Ancient history; Archaeology; Classical studies; Political sociology
contentRead.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
contentRead.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

courseLedger.contribution: Actual civic/archaeological inquiry,democratic participation/exclusion,architecture inhistoricalcontext andcollectiveMiddelburg culturalproject support people/place/civicspace. Not architecturaldesign or contemporaryplanningstudio.

courseLedger.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean

contentRead.description2: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

courseLedger.contribution: Description explicitly includes Renaissance architecture alongside painting/sculpture and global trade/colonial exchange. Full contribution to architecture-in-society/history recognized; not a complete architecture-history sequence.
